title: How Should Teachers Be Prepared?RL on Student-Induced States for On-Policy Distillation

paper.title: How Should Teachers Be Prepared? RL on Student-Induced States for On-Policy Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) improves the reasoning capabilities of small language models through token-level teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories.
Yet can teachers that excel at solving problems independently also guide student reasoning effectively?
Prior work shows that when student prefixes follow reasoning paths that differ from the teacher’s own or contain errors, teachers can be less accurate when continuing from these prefixes than when solving problems independently.
To this end, we propose Prep-OPD, which uses reinforcement learning (RL) before distillation to train the teacher to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise.
Training optimizes teacher continuations from fixed student prefixes using final-answer correctness as the reward.
The prepared teacher then trains the student through trajectory guidance and token-level supervision.
We evaluate Prep-OPD on eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, using Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the teacher and Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B as students.
With the 4B teacher and 1.7B student, Prep-OPD improves average accuracy over standard OPD and the strongest baseline, Relay-OPD, by 8.28 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively.
Controlled experiments further show that teacher RL conditioned on student-generated prefixes yields higher student accuracy than problem-start teacher RL with and without handoff on Qwen3-1.7B. Reusing the same prepared teacher also improves Qwen3-0.6B.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a promising approach for transferring reasoning capabilities from strong language models to smaller students. The student generates its own trajectories, while the teacher provides dense, token-level supervision on student-generated prefixes, often through reverse KL minimization ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . Training on student-generated trajectories helps reduce the distribution mismatch between the prefixes seen during training and those produced at inference ( Lin et al., 2020 ) . OPD can also achieve competitive reasoning performance at substantially lower training cost than a reinforcement learning (RL) baseline ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ) . However, OPD implicitly relies on the teacher being a reliable supervisor on student-generated reasoning states. This assumption can break down when student prefixes follow reasoning paths different from those the teacher would take independently, or have already gone in the wrong direction. In such cases, the teacher can be substantially less accurate when continuing from these prefixes than when solving the same problems from scratch. Its token-level feedback may also be noisy or even misleading ( Koo et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026b ) . Thus, strong independent problem-solving ability does not ensure reliable guidance on student prefixes (Figure 1 (a)). Figure 1: Motivation and main results. (a) A solution from scratch and two continuations from the same erroneous student prefix. (b) Qwen3-1.7B mean benchmark accuracy (%; Table 1 ). Existing work improves teacher guidance in several ways. Veto stabilizes optimization through adaptive distillation targets, but remains constrained by the teacher’s existing continuation capabilities ( Jang et al., 2026 ) . ESR and FastOPD concentrate supervision on early prefixes where teacher guidance is more effective, but exclude reasoning steps beyond the truncation point from distillation supervision for that training instance ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . TRD improves distillation samples by rewriting complete student trajectories, whereas SKD and Relay-OPD introduce teacher-generated tokens or segments during rollouts to intervene in student trajectories ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . However, even with early intervention, teacher continuations may still be influenced by errors in the student’s reasoning. These methods do not explicitly train the teacher to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. This suggests a simple but different strategy: prepare the teacher for student-generated reasoning states before using it for distillation . To this end, we propose Prep-OPD, which uses reinforcement learning to train the teacher to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. We then distill this ability into the student. We sample prefixes at different reasoning stages from trajectories generated by the initial student. The teacher continues reasoning while preserving each prefix and is trained through reinforcement learning with final-answer correctness as the reward, yielding the prepared teacher T P T_{P} . We then freeze and reuse the same T P T_{P} : it supplies bounded continuations at selected intermediate states in fresh student rollouts and provides token-level distillation supervision over the entire trajectory jointly generated by the student and teacher. The teacher’s continuations both provide context for the student’s subsequent reasoning and contribute directly to its updates, allowing the student to learn to build on existing reasoning and adjust its direction when needed. Inference uses only the student model (Figure 2 ). • Through controlled continuation experiments, we find that teachers can be substantially less accurate when continuing from student prefixes than when solving independently, and this gap persists even at early prefix positions. Problem-start RL improves the teacher’s independent problem-solving accuracy but provides limited gains in continuation from student prefixes. Compared with the problem-start RL teacher, the prepared teacher narrows this gap and improves mean continuation accuracy by 2.55 percentage points . • We propose Prep-OPD , which uses reinforcement learning to prepare the teacher before distillation. Conditioned on student-generated reasoning prefixes and rewarded for final-answer correctness, the teacher learns to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. The prepared teacher then distills its learned continuation ability into the student through trajectory guidance and token-level supervision. • Under a unified evaluation protocol, we evaluate Prep-OPD on eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks with two student sizes. With the 4B teacher and 1.7B student, Prep-OPD improves average accuracy over standard OPD and the strongest baseline, Relay-OPD, by 8.28 and 2.30 percentage points , respectively. sections.heading: 2 Teacher Supervision on Student Trajectories
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on trajectories sampled from its own policy, while a fixed teacher provides token-level supervision ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Let S θ S_{\theta} denote the student, S θ ¯ S_{\bar{\theta}} its rollout policy, and T T the teacher. Given a problem x x , the student generates y = ( y 1 , … , y N ) ∼ S θ ¯ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , h t = ( x , y < t ) . y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{N})\sim S_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x),\qquad h_{t}=(x,y_{<t}). (1) Standard OPD typically employs the reverse KL divergence. Taking a single-sample estimate at the student-sampled token y t y_{t} , the teacher–student log-probability difference defines the token-level advantage A ^ t OPD = log ⁡ T ⁡ ( y t ∣ h t ) − log ⁡ S θ ¯ ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) . \widehat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{OPD}}=\log T(y_{t}\mid h_{t})-\log S_{\bar{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t}). (2) A positive advantage increases the probability of the sampled token, whereas a negative one decreases it. By conditioning supervision on h t h_{t} , OPD grounds learning in the reasoning states actually visited by the student rather than exclusively in teacher-generated trajectories. However, student-generated reasoning may contain errors or commit to unproductive directions, which can compromise subsequent teacher supervision ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026b ) . In such cases, the teacher must provide useful guidance while inheriting the reasoning already produced by the student, rather than solving the problem again from a clean starting point. A teacher’s ability to solve problems from scratch therefore does not, by itself, establish its ability to provide effective supervision under student-generated reasoning. This motivates explicitly preparing the teacher to continue toward correct solutions from student-induced reasoning states.

sections.heading: 3 Prep-OPD
sections.text: To address this requirement, we propose Prep-OPD , a two-stage framework that first uses reinforcement learning to train the teacher to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise, and then reuses the same prepared teacher to guide and supervise student learning. In Stage 1 , we condition the teacher on student-generated reasoning prefixes and optimize only its continuations, using final-answer correctness as the reward, yielding the prepared teacher T P T_{P} (Sections 3.1 – 3.2 ). In Stage 2 , we freeze and reuse the same T P T_{P} to guide student trajectories through bounded continuations and provide token-level distillation supervision over the entire trajectory jointly generated by the student and teacher (Section 3.3 ). Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework.

sections.heading: 3.1 Student-Conditioned Continuation Tasks
sections.text: To prepare the teacher to adapt to reasoning states actually generated by the student, we extract unfinished reasoning prefixes from trajectories of a fixed initial student S 0 S_{0} to construct student-conditioned continuation tasks. Let 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denote a dataset of problems x x paired with reference answers a a . For each problem, we first sample a student response and then retain an unfinished prefix corresponding to an intermediate reasoning state: ( x , a ) ∼ 𝒟 , y ∼ S 0 ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , k ∼ κ ( ⋅ ∣ y ) , p = y 1 : k , (x,a)\sim\mathcal{D},\qquad y\sim S_{0}(\cdot\mid x),\qquad k\sim\kappa(\cdot\mid y),\qquad p=y_{1:k}, (3) where κ \kappa is a cut-point distribution over valid intermediate positions. Repeating this procedure yields a fixed empirical distribution q 0 q_{0} over continuation tasks ( x , p , a ) (x,p,a) . Each task asks the teacher to continue from the inherited student reasoning p p , rather than solve the problem again from a clean starting point. The reference answer a a is not exposed to the teacher and is used only to evaluate the resulting continuation. Importantly, p p remains fixed throughout the task: the teacher cannot delete or rewrite reasoning already produced by the student, and any adjustment must therefore be expressed through subsequent tokens. Sampling cut points at different depths exposes the teacher to student reasoning states from different stages of a trajectory, ranging from relatively early partial solutions to more developed reasoning contexts.

sections.text: Given continuation tasks sampled from q 0 q_{0} , we train the teacher to continue toward correct solutions while inheriting the student’s existing reasoning p p . Let T 0 T_{0} denote the initial teacher, and initialize a trainable teacher T ϕ T_{\phi} from T 0 T_{0} . Rather than restarting from the original problem, the teacher continues directly from the inherited student state: z ∼ T ϕ ( ⋅ ∣ x , p ) , z\sim T_{\phi}(\cdot\mid x,p), (4) where z z denotes the teacher-generated continuation. The completed response is p ⊕ z p\oplus z , and we optimize J prep ​ ( ϕ ) = 𝔼 ( x , p , a ) ∼ q 0 z ∼ T ϕ ( ⋅ ∣ x , p ) ​ [ R ⁡ ( x , p ⊕ z , a ) ] , J_{\mathrm{prep}}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,p,a)\sim q_{0}\\ z\sim T_{\phi}(\cdot\mid x,p)\end{subarray}}\left[R(x,p\oplus z,a)\right], (5) where R ∈ { 0 , 1 } R\in\{0,1\} evaluates final-answer correctness. This formulation separates what is inherited from what can still be changed: p p fixes the reasoning already produced by the student, whereas z z is the continuation controlled by the teacher. Final-answer correctness then rewards continuations that successfully carry the inherited student state toward a correct solution.

sections.heading: 3.3 On-Policy Distillation with the Prepared Teacher
sections.text: Having learned to continue from inherited student reasoning, the frozen T P T_{P} is reused in Stage 2 in two complementary roles: at selected states, it contributes continuations that steer the student rollout toward more reliable reasoning directions; over the resulting mixed trajectory, it provides token-level supervision. At each handoff, the prefix of the current mixed trajectory plays the same role as p p in Stage 1: it is preserved as inherited reasoning, while T P T_{P} determines what comes next. Following Relay-OPD ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , we use bounded teacher handoffs to insert continuations at selected prefixes of the mixed trajectory. During a student segment, while the handoff budget remains, T P T_{P} takes over when its most likely next token is a reflection token ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) and no reflection token appears among the rollout student S θ ¯ S_{\bar{\theta}} ’s top- 5 5 next-token candidates at the same prefix. Equation 14 in Appendix A.2 specifies this criterion; the same appendix defines the reflection-token set and handoff budgets. At a handoff, T P T_{P} emits the preferred reflection token and then samples a bounded continuation. After this segment, control returns to the student unless the rollout has terminated. The resulting mixed trajectory τ = ( τ 1 , … , τ N ) \tau=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{N}) contains both student- and teacher-generated tokens. The same frozen T P T_{P} then provides OPD supervision over the mixed trajectory. For h t τ = ( x , τ < t ) h_{t}^{\tau}=(x,\tau_{<t}) , we define A ^ t P = sg ⁡ [ log ⁡ T P ​ ( τ t ∣ h t τ ) − log ⁡ S θ ¯ ​ ( τ t ∣ h t τ ) ] , \widehat{A}_{t}^{P}=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\log T_{P}(\tau_{t}\mid h_{t}^{\tau})-\log S_{\bar{\theta}}(\tau_{t}\mid h_{t}^{\tau})\right], (9) where sg \operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. We optimize all realized response tokens with a clipped sampled-token distillation surrogate; the complete student update, token averaging, and rollout budgets are specified in Appendix A . Teacher-generated continuations therefore both shape the contexts from which the student resumes generation and participate directly in the student update, while the same T P T_{P} provides dense token-level supervision over the full mixed trajectory. After distillation, T P T_{P} is removed and inference uses the student alone.

sections.heading: Models and datasets.
sections.text: We use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the initial teacher T 0 T_{0} and Qwen3-1.7B as the primary student S 0 S_{0} , with an additional Qwen3-0.6B setting ( Yang and others, 2025 ) . Training problems come from the English subset of DAPO-Math-17K ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Both student distillation settings use 16,164 16{,}164 problems, while the GRPO stage of teacher preparation uses a 2,048 2{,}048 -problem training subset. We evaluate on the eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks used by Xu et al. (2026) : AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AIME 2026, AMC 2023, HMMT February 2026, HMMT November 2025, OlympiadBench, and MATH-500.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We include the initial student as a reference and compare with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , Standard OPD ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , TRD ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , IW-OPD ( Xie et al., 2026b ) , FastOPD ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and Relay-OPD ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . In the main Qwen3-1.7B comparison, the distillation baselines use T B T_{B} , obtained by problem-start RL from T 0 T_{0} , whereas Prep-OPD uses T P T_{P} , trained on prefixes from S 0 S_{0} . The two RL-trained teachers use the same training-problem pool and outcome verifier. For Qwen3-0.6B, we use the original teacher T 0 T_{0} for TRD because it yielded higher student accuracy than the problem-start RL teacher T B T_{B} in this full-trajectory rewriting setting. The other distillation baselines in Table 1 use T B T_{B} . Relay-OPD comparisons using T 0 T_{0} at both student sizes are reported separately in Appendix A.6 .

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: We implement training with verl and vLLM on H20 GPUs, with thinking disabled for both students. Teacher preparation runs for 128 128 GRPO steps; student distillation at both sizes uses one epoch. We use a 16,384 16{,}384 -token generation cap throughout training and evaluation; FastOPD truncates its training rollouts at 4,096 4{,}096 tokens. Training and evaluation use temperature 1.0 1.0 and top- p p 1.0 1.0 . For each training configuration, we select the student checkpoint with the highest accuracy on a development set. We evaluate the selected checkpoint using 32 32 responses per problem on the six smaller benchmarks and 4 4 on OlympiadBench and MATH-500. We report mean sampled-response accuracy and its unweighted mean across the eight benchmarks, giving each benchmark equal weight regardless of size. For the main results, we compute all eight-benchmark means and between-method differences before rounding. Training hyperparameters are summarized in Table 3 ; further implementation and evaluation details are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Student gains with and without teacher handoffs.
sections.text: Without teacher handoffs, replacing the problem-start-RL teacher T B T_{B} with the prepared teacher T P T_{P} increases average student accuracy from 39.37 % 39.37\% to 41.26 % 41.26\% ( + 1.90 +1.90 percentage points; Table 2 (a)). Both configurations use Standard OPD, where the teacher provides only token-level supervision on student-generated trajectories. The observed gain therefore does not require teacher-generated interventions. With handoffs enabled in both configurations, the same teacher replacement improves accuracy from 45.35 % 45.35\% to 47.65 % 47.65\% ( + 2.30 +2.30 points). These comparisons support the downstream value of teacher preparation over problem-start teacher RL in both settings: when the teacher serves solely as a supervisor and when it also participates in trajectory generation. Reading across rows, handoffs improve accuracy for every teacher, while T P T_{P} achieves the highest accuracy in both columns.

sections.heading: Teacher roles in generation and supervision.
sections.text: Table 2 (b) examines the prepared teacher’s value in each role. Generation includes the handoff decision and teacher segment, whereas supervision scores every realized response token. Each configuration trains its own student online and induces its own rollout distribution. Comparisons between these configurations measure conditional effects rather than independent contributions of the two roles. Holding the supervision teacher fixed at T B T_{B} , replacing the generation teacher T B T_{B} with T P T_{P} increases average student accuracy from 45.35 % 45.35\% to 46.67 % 46.67\% (approximately 1.32 1.32 percentage points). Holding the generation teacher fixed at T P T_{P} , replacing the supervision teacher T B T_{B} with T P T_{P} increases average student accuracy from 46.67 % 46.67\% to 47.65 % 47.65\% (approximately 0.98 0.98 percentage points). Together, these comparisons support the value of the prepared teacher in both trajectory generation and token-level supervision.

sections.heading: On-policy distillation.
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) builds on knowledge distillation, which transfers teacher distributions or generated sequences to a student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . For LLM post-training, OPD evaluates teacher predictions along student-generated rollouts, combining on-policy sampling with dense supervision through token-level divergence losses such as KL ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Related distillation methods refine student-data reuse and contrastive objectives ( Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) , interpolate teacher–student distributions ( Shing et al., 2025 ) , or use teacher-derived token advantages for preference alignment ( Gao et al., 2025 ) . By comparison, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) often uses sparse binary outcome rewards, which cannot distinguish among failed responses ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns from fixed demonstrations rather than trajectories sampled by the current student.

sections.heading: Supervision failure on student prefixes.
sections.text: Teacher continuation advantages can diminish as student prefixes lengthen ( Li et al., 2026 ) . More broadly, teacher hacking shows that closer imitation of an imperfect teacher on fixed offline data can increase divergence from an oracle ( Tiapkin et al., 2025 ) . Complementary distillation methods select difficult positions and adapt temperatures using teacher–student discrepancy ( Xie et al., 2026a ) , gate token-level losses through teacher verification of student proposals ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , or adjust forward/reverse KL contributions for individual vocabulary entries ( Jung et al., 2025 ) . At the trajectory level, bounded teacher handoffs alter the student’s subsequent reasoning states ( Xu et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Teacher adaptation and privileged supervision.
sections.text: Distillation with privileged context conditions teacher supervision on reference solutions, demonstrations, or environmental feedback ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . CGD trains students to refine flawed responses using teacher critiques available only during training ( Kapusuzoglu et al., 2026 ) . Other work jointly optimizes privileged and unprivileged policies with shared parameters ( Penaloza et al., 2026 ) . SD-Zero first trains a reward-conditioned reviser through supervised fine-tuning and then distills it on policy, whereas PAST applies teacher RL conditioned on complete failed attempts and reference solutions ( He et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . Prep-OPD optimizes teacher continuations from fixed intermediate student prefixes using suffix-only GRPO, with reference answers used solely to compute outcome rewards. The prepared teacher is frozen during student training to provide trajectory guidance and token-level supervision.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented Prep-OPD, which uses reinforcement learning to prepare teachers for continuation from student-generated reasoning prefixes. The prepared teacher guides student trajectories and provides token-level supervision, improving student accuracy across eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two student sizes. Our results show that stronger independent problem-solving ability does not necessarily imply better continuation from student prefixes. Controlled comparisons further show that student-prefix preparation improves continuation accuracy and benefits student learning both with and without handoffs. Role comparisons support its value in both trajectory generation and token-level supervision. The same prepared teacher also improves the smaller student, supporting reuse across the two tested student sizes.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: The implementation uses a fixed stack (verl 0.9.0, vLLM 0.21.0) and a versioned data pipeline: the corpus is deduplicated to 17,188 17{,}188 problems with a manifest recording every removal, and prefix states carry exact token IDs with recorded cut indices and exclusion statistics. The main results use seed 42; additional student runs are reported in Appendix A.7 . Teacher and student protocols are described in Section 4.1 and Appendix A , including checkpoint selection on a development set and evaluation on the eight-benchmark suite. Evaluation uses the released benchmark runner of the base repository. We will release code, configurations, manifests, and the prefix-state construction tooling in an anonymous repository at submission.

sections.heading: Models and input representation.
sections.text: We use the unmodified Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B checkpoint as S 0 S_{0} and Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as T 0 T_{0} . The same fixed S 0 S_{0} checkpoint supplies the student-generated reasoning prefixes and initializes the trainable student S θ S_{\theta} ; the trainable teacher T ϕ T_{\phi} is initialized from T 0 T_{0} . The system message is “Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{} .” The user message contains the problem. We render these messages with the fixed student tokenizer, using add_generation_prompt=True and enable_thinking=False . Teacher continuation inputs concatenate the stored prompt and prefix token IDs directly, continuing the same unfinished assistant response without re-rendering the prefix or adding a new assistant turn. The reference answer is stored in a separate verifier field. Model and tokenizer revisions are fixed across stages, and rendered input IDs are retained with each task. Token-ID sharing requires compatible token-to-ID mappings, including the special tokens used for generation and stopping, across both models.

Each path must establish answer equivalence to yield reward 1 1 ; successful extraction alone is not sufficient. The reward is 0 0 if no path establishes equivalence or grading raises an exception. Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) improves the reasoning capabilities of small language models through token-level teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories. Yet can teachers that excel at solving problems independently also guide student reasoning effectively? Prior work shows that when student prefixes follow reasoning paths that differ from the teacher’s own or contain errors, teachers can be less accurate when continuing from these prefixes than when solving problems independently. To this end, we propose Prep-OPD, which uses reinforcement learning (RL) before distillation to train the teacher to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. Training optimizes teacher continuations from fixed student prefixes using final-answer correctness as the reward. The prepared teacher then trains the student through trajectory guidance and token-level supervision. We evaluate Prep-OPD on eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, using Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the teacher and Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B as students. With the 4B teacher and 1.7B student, Prep-OPD improves average accuracy over standard OPD and the strongest baseline, Relay-OPD, by 8.28 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively. Controlled experiments further show that teacher RL conditioned on student-generated prefixes yields higher student accuracy than problem-start teacher RL with and without handoff on Qwen3-1.7B. Reusing the same prepared teacher also improves Qwen3-0.6B. 1 Introduction On-policy distillation (OPD) is a promising approach for transferring reasoning capabilities from strong language models to smaller students. The student generates its own trajectories, while the teacher provides dense, token-level supervision on student-generated prefixes, often through reverse KL minimization ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . Training on student-generated trajectories helps reduce the distribution mismatch between the prefixes seen during training and those produced at inference ( Lin et al., 2020 ) . OPD can also achieve competitive reasoning performance at substantially lower training cost than a reinforcement learning (RL) baseline ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ) . However, OPD implicitly relies on the teacher being a reliable supervisor on student-generated reasoning states. This assumption can break down when student prefixes follow reasoning paths different from those the teacher would take independently, or have already gone in the wrong direction. In such cases, the teacher can be substantially less accurate when continuing from these prefixes than when solving the same problems from scratch. Its token-level feedback may also be noisy or even misleading ( Koo et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026b ) . Thus, strong independent problem-solving ability does not ensure reliable guidance on student prefixes (Figure 1 (a)). Figure 1: Motivation and main results. (a) A solution from scratch and two continuations from the same erroneous student prefix. (b) Qwen3-1.7B mean benchmark accuracy (%; Table 1 ). Existing work improves teacher guidance in several ways. Veto stabilizes optimization through adaptive distillation targets, but remains constrained by the teacher’s existing continuation capabilities ( Jang et al., 2026 ) . ESR and FastOPD concentrate supervision on early prefixes where teacher guidance is more effective, but exclude reasoning steps beyond the truncation point from distillation supervision for that training instance ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . TRD improves distillation samples by rewriting complete student trajectories, whereas SKD and Relay-OPD introduce teacher-generated tokens or segments during rollouts to intervene in student trajectories ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . However, even with early intervention, teacher continuations may still be influenced by errors in the student’s reasoning. These methods do not explicitly train the teacher to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. This suggests a simple but different strategy: prepare the teacher for student-generated reasoning states before using it for distillation . To this end, we propose Prep-OPD, which uses reinforcement learning to train the teacher to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. We then distill this ability into the student. We sample prefixes at different reasoning stages from trajectories generated by the initial student. The teacher continues reasoning while preserving each prefix and is trained through reinforcement learning with final-answer correctness as the reward, yielding the prepared teacher T P T_{P} . We then freeze and reuse the same T P T_{P} : it supplies bounded continuations at selected intermediate states in fresh student rollouts and provides token-level distillation supervision over the entire trajectory jointly generated by the student and teacher. The teacher’s continuations both provide context for the student’s subsequent reasoning and contribute directly to its updates, allowing the student to learn to build on existing reasoning and adjust its direction when needed. Inference uses only the student model (Figure 2 ). • Through controlled continuation experiments, we find that teachers can be substantially less accurate when continuing from student prefixes than when solving independently, and this gap persists even at early prefix positions. Problem-start RL improves the teacher’s independent problem-solving accuracy but provides limited gains in continuation from student prefixes. Compared with the problem-start RL teacher, the prepared teacher narrows this gap and improves mean continuation accuracy by 2.55 percentage points . • We propose Prep-OPD , which uses reinforcement learning to prepare the teacher before distillation. Conditioned on student-generated reasoning prefixes and rewarded for final-answer correctness, the teacher learns to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. The prepared teacher then distills its learned continuation ability into the student through trajectory guidance and token-level supervision. • Under a unified evaluation protocol, we evaluate Prep-OPD on eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks with two student sizes. With the 4B teacher and 1.7B student, Prep-OPD improves average accuracy over standard OPD and the strongest baseline, Relay-OPD, by 8.28 and 2.30 percentage points , respectively. Inference uses the student alone. 2 Teacher Supervision on Student Trajectories On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on trajectories sampled from its own policy, while a fixed teacher provides token-level supervision ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Let S θ S_{\theta} denote the student, S θ ¯ S_{\bar{\theta}} its rollout policy, and T T the teacher. Given a problem x x , the student generates y = ( y 1 , … , y N ) ∼ S θ ¯ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , h t = ( x , y < t ) . y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{N})\sim S_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x),\qquad h_{t}=(x,y_{<t}). (1) Standard OPD typically employs the reverse KL divergence. Taking a single-sample estimate at the student-sampled token y t y_{t} , the teacher–student log-probability difference defines the token-level advantage A ^ t OPD = log ⁡ T ⁡ ( y t ∣ h t ) − log ⁡ S θ ¯ ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) . \widehat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{OPD}}=\log T(y_{t}\mid h_{t})-\log S_{\bar{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t}). (2) A positive advantage increases the probability of the sampled token, whereas a negative one decreases it. By conditioning supervision on h t h_{t} , OPD grounds learning in the reasoning states actually visited by the student rather than exclusively in teacher-generated trajectories. However, student-generated reasoning may contain errors or commit to unproductive directions, which can compromise subsequent teacher supervision ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026b ) . In such cases, the teacher must provide useful guidance while inheriting the reasoning already produced by the student, rather than solving the problem again from a clean starting point. A teacher’s ability to solve problems from scratch therefore does not, by itself, establish its ability to provide effective supervision under student-generated reasoning. This motivates explicitly preparing the teacher to continue toward correct solutions from student-induced reasoning states. 3 Prep-OPD To address this requirement, we propose Prep-OPD , a two-stage framework that first uses reinforcement learning to train the teacher to adapt to the student’s existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise, and then reuses the same prepared teacher to guide and supervise student learning. In Stage 1 , we condition the teacher on student-generated reasoning prefixes and optimize only its continuations, using final-answer correctness as the reward, yielding the prepared teacher T P T_{P} (Sections 3.1 – 3.2 ). In Stage 2 , we freeze and reuse the same T P T_{P} to guide student trajectories through bounded continuations and provide token-level distillation supervision over the entire trajectory jointly generated by the student and teacher (Section 3.3 ). Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework. 3.1 Student-Conditioned Continuation Tasks To prepare the teacher to adapt to reasoning states actually generated by the student, we extract unfinished reasoning prefixes from trajectories of a fixed initial student S 0 S_{0} to construct student-conditioned continuation tasks. Let 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denote a dataset of problems x x paired with reference answers a a . For each problem, we first sample a student response and then retain an unfinished prefix corresponding to an intermediate reasoning state: ( x , a ) ∼ 𝒟 , y ∼ S 0 ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , k ∼ κ ( ⋅ ∣ y ) , p = y 1 : k , (x,a)\sim\mathcal{D},\qquad y\sim S_{0}(\cdot\mid x),\qquad k\sim\kappa(\cdot\mid y),\qquad p=y_{1:k}, (3) where κ \kappa is a cut-point distribution over valid intermediate positions. Repeating this procedure yields a fixed empirical distribution q 0 q_{0} over continuation tasks ( x , p , a ) (x,p,a) . Each task asks the teacher to continue from the inherited student reasoning p p , rather than solve the problem again from a clean starting point. The reference answer a a is not exposed to the teacher and is used only to evaluate the resulting continuation. Importantly, p p remains fixed throughout the task: the teacher cannot delete or rewrite reasoning already produced by the student, and any adjustment must therefore be expressed through subsequent tokens. Sampling cut points at different depths exposes the teacher to student reasoning states from different stages of a trajectory, ranging from relatively early partial solutions to more developed reasoning contexts. 3.2 Teacher Preparation via Reinforcement Learning Teacher preparation objective. On-policy distillation (OPD) builds on knowledge distillation, which transfers teacher distributions or generated sequences to a student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . For LLM post-training, OPD evaluates teacher predictions along student-generated rollouts, combining on-policy sampling with dense supervision through token-level divergence losses such as KL ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Related distillation methods refine student-data reuse and contrastive objectives ( Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) , interpolate teacher–student distributions ( Shing et al., 2025 ) , or use teacher-derived token advantages for preference alignment ( Gao et al., 2025 ) . By comparison, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) often uses sparse binary outcome rewards, which cannot distinguish among failed responses ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns from fixed demonstrations rather than trajectories sampled by the current student. Supervision failure on student prefixes. Teacher continuation advantages can diminish as student prefixes lengthen ( Li et al., 2026 ) . More broadly, teacher hacking shows that closer imitation of an imperfect teacher on fixed offline data can increase divergence from an oracle ( Tiapkin et al., 2025 ) . Complementary distillation methods select difficult positions and adapt temperatures using teacher–student discrepancy ( Xie et al., 2026a ) , gate token-level losses through teacher verification of student proposals ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , or adjust forward/reverse KL contributions for individual vocabulary entries ( Jung et al., 2025 ) . At the trajectory level, bounded teacher handoffs alter the student’s subsequent reasoning states ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . Teacher adaptation and privileged supervision. Distillation with privileged context conditions teacher supervision on reference solutions, demonstrations, or environmental feedback ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . CGD trains students to refine flawed responses using teacher critiques available only during training ( Kapusuzoglu et al., 2026 ) . Other work jointly optimizes privileged and unprivileged policies with shared parameters ( Penaloza et al., 2026 ) . SD-Zero first trains a reward-conditioned reviser through supervised fine-tuning and then distills it on policy, whereas PAST applies teacher RL conditioned on complete failed attempts and reference solutions ( He et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . Prep-OPD optimizes teacher continuations from fixed intermediate student prefixes using suffix-only GRPO, with reference answers used solely to compute outcome rewards. The prepared teacher is frozen during student training to provide trajectory guidance and token-level supervision. 6 Conclusion We presented Prep-OPD, which uses reinforcement learning to prepare teachers for continuation from student-generated reasoning prefixes. The prepared teacher guides student trajectories and provides token-level supervision, improving student accuracy across eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two student sizes. Our results show that stronger independent problem-solving ability does not necessarily imply better continuation from student prefixes. Controlled comparisons further show that student-prefix preparation improves continuation accuracy and benefits student learning both with and without handoffs. Role comparisons support its value in both trajectory generation and token-level supervision. The same prepared teacher also improves the smaller student, supporting reuse across the two tested student sizes.
